DRE-3164 is the epic the seam rule was WRITTEN FROM (DRE-3244,
standards/card-quality.md '## When a plan is two epics'): thirteen build
cards under one parent, an [OPERATOR] card in the middle of the chain, and
a surfaces table saying the relay joins 'second, after a week of clean
console releases'. It is the body every seam tell can be read off, which
is what makes it a fixture rather than an invented one.
The body is the Linear description as it stood BEFORE the 2026-09-06
split, so the paragraph opening '**Split on 2026-09-06' — written after
it — is dropped; everything from '**The CEO, 2026-09-05 10:00 PT:**' on
is the original text. Linear markdown links are flattened to their titles,
as the DRE-3013 fixture does; nothing else is edited.
DRE-3394-EIGHT is the control: an ordinary eight-card epic with no
observation phrase anywhere in it, so the classifier's decision for it must
be byte-for-byte what it was before the seam reading existed. Synthetic on
purpose — a real card carrying no seam is easy to find and easy to have
`expect` is the shape the classifier must stamp; `why` is why.

cards.title: [EPIC] The release train — one reusable train in bureau-pipeline, a thin stub per repo, every deploy surface in the fleet rolling out by itself: one lane per surface, triggers collapse, spaced, inside the hours, on each repo's own rollout script and rollback
cards.body:
**The CEO, 2026-09-05 10:00 PT:** *"Is there any way we can get the deployment faster, while still keeping it to the same standard of quality?"* On the train: *"That is a great design, do it."* And at 10:19 PT: *"We should use this same approach for other projects (portico, bureau pipeline, etc.). It should be releasing all the time. It should be a general train that is always running for all projects."*

## The finding

The slow part of a deploy is not the deploy; it is the wait for a person to run it. Read on 2026-09-05 for the console: CI already builds and pushes both images on every console merge (`console-release.yml`, `AWS_DEPLOY_ENABLED=true` since 06-20); `infra/deploy-console.sh` takes the CI-built image, runs migrations in the one-shot task, rolls out only the services whose digest changed, waits for App Runner to confirm (bounded, aborting loud with the rollback printed), and tags — about ten minutes, most of it the platform. Releases were cut about once a day. The same is true of every surface: the website is 16 commits behind, the relay was 4 behind until this morning, and each waits on a hand.

The quality bar sits BEFORE the merge — CI, the critic's APPROVE, the verifier, the merge gate — and none of it changes if the rollout runs itself. The deploy adds only the rollout check and the rollback, and those are the same code either way.

## The design (decided with the CEO, 2026-09-05)

**One train, the house shape: a reusable workflow in** `bureau-pipeline`**, a thin stub per repo.** Exactly how the other eight stubs work (DRE-2553): the stub rides `@stable`, passes `pipeline_ref: stable`, the scaffold ships it, and `make check-channel-fleet` keeps it on the channel. The train contains no product's deploy steps; every product declares its surfaces as DATA and owns the script that rolls each one out.

1. **The data.** Each repo carries `.github/bureau/release.json`: per surface — name, the tag series, the paths that count as "changed", the release script the repo owns (`infra/release-<surface>.sh`: migrations, rollout, verify, tag, in that repo's own terms), the rollback command, the spacing, the window, and the identity it runs under. `scripts/check_deploy_lag.py`'s surface table becomes this data, read from every repo, so the deploy-lag report and the train read one fact (`adr-one-writer-per-fact`).
2. **The train, per surface.** One lane (`concurrency: release:<repo>:<surface>`, never cancel-in-progress). Triggers collapse: a release deploys the head of the default branch when it starts, so merges that land during a rollout become the next release, not one each. Spacing: at most one release per **30 minutes** per surface (read from the newest tag), and a no-op that says so when the surface already reads current. Window: **07:00–21:00 PT** with a 07:00 batch for overnight merges; a surface may declare `always` in its data. Green at that SHA, or a refusal that says so.
3. **Same steps as the operator's script, from one implementation.** The repo's release script is the one rollout implementation; the operator's `make deploy-<surface>` becomes a local caller of it and refuses while a train release is in flight.
4. **Receipts.** Every release posts one line to the deploy log the console shows (Shipped today → Pending release empties itself); a failed or reverted release raises a CRITICAL alert on the Alerts feed and cuts no tag. Never a silent retry.
5. **Two hand brakes.** Per surface, `auto: false` in the data. Fleet-wide, one variable in `bureau-pipeline` in the shape of `INTAKE_HOLD`, read by the reusable train, so the operator can stop every train with one switch.
6. **Where the identity lives.** Each repo's stub runs under that repo's own cloud identity (OIDC role), granted by that repo's operator. The train never holds a fleet-wide deploy credential.

## The surfaces, in the order they join

| surface | today | what joins |
| -- | -- | -- |
| agent-bureau · console | CI builds images; the operator rolls out by hand | **the pilot** — `release.json`, the stub, `release-console.sh` shared with `deploy-console.sh` (pre-filed) |
| agent-bureau · relay | `cloud/relay/deploy.sh` by hand | second, after a week of clean console releases |
| agent-bureau · website | `make deploy-website` by hand (build → S3 → CloudFront → tag) | same shape as the relay |
| bureau-pipeline · the `stable` channel | **already a train** — `promote-channel.yml` advances `stable` on every harness-proven commit (DRE-2551), with its alarm (DRE-2552) | stays as it is; declared as a surface so deploy-lag and the receipts read it the same way |
| portico · the portals | per-AWS-account Lambda@Edge stack + S3 publish, by hand (the `deploy-portico-account` procedure) | its script is that procedure; its operator grants the identity; the cut-over portals' redirect stubs are the known hazard |
| atlas, deltasolv | their own orgs and AWS | the stub installs with the scaffold; nothing rolls until that product's operator grants the identity and flips `auto` |

## What is operator-owned inside this

* Per surface: the identity grant (an agent writes the policy, the operator applies it), one supervised train release, then the flip. The console's is pre-filed; the others are one card each, filed when their turn comes.

## Constraints that are not negotiable

* The gates in front of the merge do not change.
* A repo's release script runs its migrations before any service rolls, and a failed migration aborts the release.
* No product's deploy steps live in the train, and no second copy of any product's steps. The stub is data plus one `uses:` line.
* The train never deploys a default branch whose CI is not green at that commit.
* Rollback stays that surface's one command, unchanged.
* Another project's release process is touched only through its own stub and its own operator card — never from here.

## Three children are pre-filed — wire to them, do not re-file

1. **bureau-pipeline: the reusable train** — the `workflow_call`, the `release.json` schema and its check, the fleet-wide brake, the collapse / spacing / window / green-at-SHA logic with a Python harness.
2. **agent-bureau: the console surface** — `release.json`, the stub, `release-console.sh` shared with `deploy-console.sh`. Blocked by 1.
3. **[OPERATOR] the console's identity grant, the supervised first release, the flip** — needs-human, no-code. Blocked by 2.

The planner adds what is left: `check_deploy_lag.py` reading the data, the deploy-log receipt and the failure alert, the scaffold shipping the stub and `check-channel-fleet` covering it, the relay and website surfaces (each blocked by a week of clean console releases), portico's card, the proof and the demo.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A merge to a repo's default branch touching a declared surface inside its window rolls out by itself within its spacing, with no human command, and deploy-lag reads current afterwards
- [ ] Four merges in ten minutes produce ONE rollout, observed on the console
- [ ] A merge at 23:00 PT rolls out at 07:00 PT, not before, observed
- [ ] A failed rollout aborts, reverts, cuts no tag and raises a CRITICAL alert
- [ ] Every surface's operator deploy and the train run the same script; the operator command refuses while a train release is in flight
- [ ] The fleet-wide brake stops every train with one switch, observed
- [ ] The train workflow lives in `bureau-pipeline`; each repo's stub is data plus one `uses:` line and rides `@stable`

**Not green-lit.** The planner reads this in Planning; the CEO approves the plan from Green Light by moving the epic to In Progress. Spacing and window are the CEO's decisions: 30 minutes and 07:00–21:00 PT to start, adjusted from what the first releases show.

cards.title: [EPIC] The Alerts panel reads by severity — the vocabulary, the engine stamp, the grouped panel and its API
cards.body:
**The CEO, 2026-09-04 09:00 PT:** *"The alerts panel is unreadable — I cannot tell a warning from a fire."*

## The finding

The console's Alerts panel renders every monitor's output in one flat list, in
the order the engine happened to emit them. A CRITICAL sits below three WARNs
and nothing says which one matters.

## The plan — eight cards under one parent

1. The severity vocabulary as data, read by the engine and the panel alike.
2. The engine stamps each raised alert with its severity from that file.
3. The panel groups by severity, criticals first.
4. The panel's row carries the monitor that raised it and when.
5. A resolved alert leaves the list rather than greying out in place.
6. The de-dupe key moves into the vocabulary beside the severity.
7. The Alerts API returns the grouped shape, so the panel does no sorting.
8. The alert-engine README is rewritten against the new shape in the same pull
   request that changes it.

Every card is one file plus its tests, and each is shippable alone. Nothing in
the list waits on anything being watched: card 3 reads card 1's file, which is
why card 1 goes first, and the rest are independent of each other.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The panel shows criticals above warnings, with the monitor and the time on
      every row
- [ ] A resolved alert disappears from the list
- [ ] The severity vocabulary is one file, read by both the engine and the API
